title: OIDC CIBA (Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication)
subtitle: A decoupled flow: the app asks the IdP to authenticate the user out-of-band on their phone, then polls for tokens — there is essentially nothing to see in a browser Network tab.

steps.label: User requests service, identifies self
steps.lede: The user asks the consumption-device client for something (e.g. authorizing a payment at a call center) and identifies themselves — here by phone number. Authentication will happen on a separate device.
steps.devtools: DevTools gets you almost nothing here — and that is the point. CIBA is decoupled and back-channel: the client talks to the IdP server-to-server and the user authenticates out-of-band on their phone. To observe it you capture on the client back end (app HTTP logs, or an egress proxy like mitmproxy), never in the browser.

steps.label: POST /bc-authorize (back-channel)
steps.lede: The client makes the backchannel authentication request: scope, exactly one identity hint (login_hint here), an optional human-readable binding_message, and client authentication (private_key_jwt). It gets back an auth_req_id to poll with.
steps.devtools: Not in the browser. Capture on the client (proxy / server logs). Exactly one of login_hint / login_hint_token / id_token_hint is allowed. The response auth_req_id is the handle you poll with; interval is the minimum seconds between polls.

steps.label: Push challenge to the user’s phone (out-of-band)
steps.lede: The IdP pushes an authentication request to the user’s registered authenticator app, showing the client name and the binding_message. This travels the device vendor’s push channel — not HTTP you can capture.
steps.devtools: Not an HTTP request you can see at all — not in DevTools, not even in your egress proxy. The user will compare the binding_message (PAY-4711) shown on both the consumption device and the phone before approving.

steps.label: POST /token — first poll (pending)
steps.lede: The client polls the token endpoint with the CIBA grant. The user hasn’t approved yet, so the IdP answers authorization_pending — keep polling at the given interval.
steps.devtools: Server-side only. Each poll sends grant_type=urn:openid:params:grant-type:ciba and auth_req_id. Responses to expect: authorization_pending (waiting), slow_down (polling too fast — add ~5s), then 200 on approval. Terminal errors: expired_token, access_denied, transaction_failed.

steps.label: User approves on the phone (out-of-band)
steps.lede: The user verifies the binding_message matches, authenticates on the phone (fingerprint + OTP), and approves. The authenticator reports the result back to the IdP — all off the browser and off your proxy.
steps.devtools: Nothing to capture: this happens entirely on the authentication device. This decoupling is CIBA’s whole value — the device requesting access and the device authorizing it are different.

steps.label: POST /token — later poll (tokens issued)
steps.lede: A subsequent poll now succeeds: the IdP returns the access token, refresh token, and an ID token whose auth_req_id claim ties it back to this exact backchannel request.

jwt.title: Decoded id_token
payload: Subject — the user who approved on their phone
When the user approved on the auth device
Fingerprint + OTP on the authentication device
Binds this id_token to THIS backchannel request — not a replay

steps.devtools: Server-side. The auth_req_id claim in the ID token equals the value returned from /bc-authorize, so the client can confirm these tokens answer its request and not a replayed one.

steps.label: Transaction proceeds
steps.lede: With valid tokens in hand, the consumption device completes the action. The browser, if any is even present, saw none of the authentication.
steps.devtools: In ping mode the IdP instead POSTs the client’s client_notification_endpoint with Authorization: Bearer <client_notification_token> to signal completion — captured on the client’s inbound (webhook) side, again never in a browser.
